en: Netti:
The Section on Detailed Exposition of the Counter-Demonstrations (Paṭiniddesavāra Vibhaṅga) 6
The Analysis of the Fourfold Array Mode (*Catubyūhahāravibhaṅga*).
Therein, what is the fourfold array mode?
It is this: "Etymology and intention."
By means of the phrasing, the etymology, the intention, the source, and the connection between what precedes and what follows, the discourse is to be investigated.
In this regard, what is etymology? It is that which is connected with terms of linguistic analysis; it is the knowledge of phenomena by way of their names.
For when a bhikkhu knows the name of the meaning and knows the name of the phenomenon, he applies it accordingly.
And he is called one skilled in meaning, skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in phrasing, skilled in etymological interpretation, skilled in what precedes and follows, skilled in teaching,
skilled in designations for the past, skilled in designations for the future, skilled in designations for the present, skilled in designations for females, skilled in designations for males,
skilled in designations for neuters, and skilled in singular designations.
One skilled in many designations [should understand] all local expressions and all local idioms in this way.
This is the compendium of terms of language (niruttipadasaṃhitā).
In that regard, what is the underlying intention (adhippāya)?
“Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives by Dhamma,
like a great umbrella in the rainy season.
This is the benefit when Dhamma is well-practiced.”
“The one who lives according to the Dhamma does not go to an unhappy destination.
What is the Blessed One’s intention here?
His intention here is this: “Those who wish to be liberated from the states of misery will become practitioners of the Dhamma.”
“Just as a bird caught at the opening of its cage is slain and bound by its own karma,
so too does this generation, having passed away, suffer in the next world.”
“By one’s own karma one is slain and bound.
What is the Blessed One’s intention here?
“One will experience the undesired, unpleasant result of intentional kamma that has been performed and accumulated, which is to be felt as suffering”—this is the Blessed One’s intention in this case.
“He who, seeking his own happiness,
harms with a stick beings who desire happiness— ”
“Having died, he does not obtain happiness.
What is the Blessed One’s intention here?
His intention here is this: “Those who will have need of happiness shall not perform evil deeds.”
“When one is drowsy and a great eater,
sleeping and tossing about in bed like a great boar fattened on fodder— ”
"The dull-witted enter the womb again and again.
What is the Blessed One’s intention here?
Those who wish to be repelled by aging and death will become moderate in their food and restrained in their sense faculties.

“Guarding the doors of the senses, devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night, possessing insight into wholesome states, and showing reverence toward fellow celibates—whether elders, juniors, or those of middle standing”: this is the Blessed One’s intended meaning here.
“Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless...”
Heedlessness is the path to death;
those who are heedful do not die,
while those who are heedless are as if already dead.
What is the Blessed One’s intention here?
His intention here is this: "Those who wish to seek the deathless will dwell with diligence.
This is the intention.
In this regard, what is the source?
It is as that cowherd Dhaniya said to the Blessed One:
"One who has sons rejoices in his sons..."
The cowherd likewise rejoices with his cattle;
for acquisitions are the joy of a man,
for he who is without acquisitions does not rejoice.
The Blessed One said:
"One who has sons grieves because of his sons;
likewise, Gopikā grieves because of her cows."
"For acquisitions are a man's sorrow;
he who is without acquisitions does not grieve.
By this passage and by this cause, it is thus understood: "In this instance, the Blessed One spoke of external possessions as 'acquisition' (upadhi)."
And when Māra the Evil One hurled down a large rock from Vulture Peak Mountain, the Blessed One said:
“Even if you were to shake the entire Vulture Peak, in its entirety...”
In those who are rightly liberated,
in the Buddhas, there is no wavering.
Even if the sky were to split and the earth were to shake,
"May all living beings indeed tremble;
even if they were to drive a stake into one's chest,
Buddhas find no refuge in acquisitions."
By this instance and by this cause, it is thus known: “Here the Blessed One has taken up the body as a substrate.
And as it is said:
“The wise do not call that a firm bond;”
That which is for iron, wood, and bamboo;
that passion and attachment for jewels and earrings,
and that longing for children and wives.
By this instance and by this cause it is thus known: “Here the Blessed One spoke of craving for external objects.
And as it is said:
“The wise call this a firm bond;”
“Carrying away, slack, and difficult to release—
having cut even this as well, they go forth as wanderers,
without longing, having abandoned sensual pleasure.”
By this instance and by this cause, it is thus understood: "Here, the Blessed One has taught the abandoning of craving for external objects.
And as it is said:
"Afflicted, impure, and putrid..."
A foul odor emanating from the body,
trickling day and night—
yet this is what fools delight in.
By this instance and by this cause it is thus known: “Here, the Blessed One has taught the abandoning of craving for internal bases.
And as it is said:
“Cut off your own affection;”
Like an autumnal white lotus with the hand,
cultivate only the path to peace—
the Nibbāna taught by the Sugata.
By this basis and by this cause, it is thus understood: "Here, the Blessed One has taught the abandoning of craving for internal bases.
This is the cause.
In that regard, what is the connection between what precedes and what follows?
As it is said:
"Blinded by ignorance, shrouded by a net,
covered by the veil of craving;"
Bound by the fetters of negligence,
like fish at the mouth of a net,
they follow after aging and death.
"Like a calf still nursing its mother"—
this is what is called craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*).
With what preceding and following [teachings] is it consistent?
As it is said:
"One who is lustful does not know the goal;
one who is lustful does not see the Dhamma."
“Then there is blinding darkness for the person whom passion overcomes. Thus,
by means of both blindness and being shrouded, that very same craving is described.
When it is said, “Blinded by desire, shrouded by a net, covered by the veil of craving,” and when it is said, “The lustful one does not know the goal;
the lustful one does not see the Dhamma,” by these words and these obsessions, that very craving is expressed.
That which is darkness is this origin of suffering; and that which is craving leading to renewed existence, and what was called “sensual pleasures”—these are the sensual desires of defilement.

And when he says, "covered with a net," he shows the obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) resulting from the application of those very same sensual desires; therefore, craving as a bond is described both by way of defilement (*kilesa*) and by way of obsession.
Those who are such as these follow after aging and death; this was shown by the Blessed One through the power of the verse as it was laid down:
"He for whom there is no proliferation (*papañca*) and no persistence..."
Having transcended the tether and the crossbar,
the world together with its devas does not recognize that thirstless sage as he wanders.
"Proliferation" (papañca) refers to craving, views, and conceit, as well as the formations conditioned by them.
"Stability" (ṭhiti) refers to the underlying tendencies (anusaya).
"Fettering" (sandāna) refers to the obsession of craving, namely the thirty-six modes of the net of craving.
"Obstacle" (paligha) means delusion (moha).
Those who have completely transcended all these—proliferated formations, persistence, bondage, the obstacle, and delusion—they are called "free from craving" (nittaṇha).

In this context, the formations of obsession are to be experienced either in the present life, in the next rebirth, or in subsequent lives; thus craving yields a threefold fruit: either in the present life, in the next rebirth, or in some later period.
Thus the Blessed One has said:
"Whatever action one performs out of greed, whether by body, speech, or mind, one experiences its result either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period.
This is consistent with what the Blessed One said earlier and later.
In that regard, "obsession" refers to karma to be experienced in this very life, karma to be experienced upon rebirth, or karma to be experienced in some subsequent period;
thus, karma ripens in three ways: either in the present life, or upon rebirth, or in a later period.
As it is said:
"If a fool here is one who takes life...
[and so on] ...and holds wrong view, he experiences the result of that either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period."
This is consistent with the sequence of the Blessed One’s teaching.

In that regard, the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) are to be abandoned by the power of reflection; the formations (*saṅkhārā*) by the power of vision; and the thirty-six modes of craving’s roaming (*taṇhāvicarita*) by the power of cultivation. Thus, craving is abandoned in three ways.
That state of being free from craving is the element of Nibbāna with residue (*saupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*).
This is the Nibbāna-element without residue, which is the dissolution of the body.
"Proliferation" (papañca) is said to be a continuous attachment.
And as the Blessed One said: "One proliferates by taking as an object a form cognizable by the eye, whether past, future, or present."
And as for what the Blessed One said:

"Rādha, be indifferent toward past form; do not delight in future form; practice for the sake of disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, for the cessation of, and for the relinquishing of present form"—this is consistent with the Blessed One’s earlier and later teachings.
Furthermore, whatever conceptual proliferation (*papañca*), whatever formations (*saṅkhārā*), and whatever delighting in the past, future, and present—these are one and the same thing.
Moreover, by means of various phrases, various syllables, and various phonemes, an immeasurable teaching of the Dhamma has been spoken by the Blessed One.
Thus, having correlated sutta with sutta and having joined it with what precedes and follows, the sutta becomes fully elucidated.

Thus, this sequence of preceding and following [terms] is fourfold: connection of meaning (*atthasandhi*), connection of phrasing (*byañjanasandhi*), connection of teaching (*desanāsandhi*), and connection of exposition (*niddesasandhi*).
Therein, the connection of meaning consists of six terms: making known, manifesting, disclosing, analyzing, clarifying, and describing.
The connection of phrasing consists of six terms: syllable, word, phrase, mode, language, and exposition.
The connection of the teaching: The meditator does not meditate depending on earth, yet he meditates;
he does not meditate depending on water, yet he meditates; he does not meditate depending on fire, yet he meditates;
he does not meditate depending on air, yet he meditates; ...pe... he does not meditate depending on the base of infinite space.

… nor does he meditate depending on the base of infinite consciousness; nor does he meditate depending on the base of nothingness; nor does he meditate depending on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
nor does he meditate depending on this world; nor does he meditate depending on the other world; yet the meditator meditates.

Furthermore, that which lies between these two—whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or reflected upon and examined by the mind—that too he does not depend upon while meditating, yet the meditator meditates.
In this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, one who meditates with an unsupported mind cannot be discerned.
Just as the Evil Māra, while searching for the consciousness of the clansman Godhika, neither knew nor saw it;
for he had transcended conceptual proliferation (*papañca*) through the abandoning of craving, and thus he had no basis for views.

And just as in the case of Godhika, so too in the case of Vakkali, while they were meditating, their minds—being unattached—were not known by the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, or by this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans.
This is the connection of the teaching (*desanā-sandhi*).
In that regard, what is the connection of the exposition (*niddesa-sandhi*)?
A mind dependent on something is to be demonstrated by way of the unwholesome side; a mind independent of anything is to be demonstrated by way of the wholesome side.
A dependent mind is to be demonstrated by way of defilement; an independent mind is to be demonstrated by way of purification.
A dependent mind is to be demonstrated by way of the occurrence of saṃsāra; an independent mind is to be demonstrated by way of the cessation of saṃsāra.
A mind dependent [on objects] is to be demonstrated by way of craving and ignorance; a mind independent is to be demonstrated by way of serenity and insight.
A mind dependent is to be demonstrated by way of shamelessness and lack of moral dread; a mind independent is to be demonstrated by way of shame and moral dread.
A mind dependent is to be demonstrated by way of unmindfulness and lack of clear comprehension; a mind independent is to be demonstrated by way of mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Those with dependent minds are to be demonstrated by way of the improper and improper attention; those with independent minds are to be demonstrated by way of the proper and proper attention.
Those with dependent minds are to be demonstrated by way of indolence and difficult speech; those with independent minds are to be demonstrated by way of the arousal of energy and easy speech.
Those with dependent minds are to be demonstrated by way of lack of faith and negligence; those with independent minds are to be demonstrated by way of faith and diligence.

Those with dependent minds are to be characterized by listening to what is not the true Dhamma and by lack of restraint; those with independent minds are to be characterized by listening to the true Dhamma and by restraint.
Those with dependent minds are to be characterized by covetousness and ill will; those with independent minds are to be characterized by non-covetousness and non-ill will.

Those with dependent minds are to be characterized by the hindrances and by the fetters; those with independent minds are to be characterized by the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust and by the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance.

Those with minds dependent on views are to be demonstrated by way of the view of annihilationism and the view of eternalism; those with minds non-dependent are to be demonstrated by way of the element of nibbāna with residue remaining and the element of nibbāna without residue remaining.
This is the connection of demonstration.
Therefore the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said: "The etymological analysis and the intended meaning."
The Fourfold Array method of exposition is concluded.
